title: Reconciliation
hookLine: a weekly check: is there anyone I need to make peace with?
tomorrow: seven boxes drawn on a page. what goes in each one?

cards: A message sits unanswered for three days, and both people are waiting for the other to go first. Jesus tells a small story about that standoff. A man stands at the altar with his offering in his hands.

He has made the trip, the moment has come, and a face drifts into his mind: someone who has something against him. Jesus' instruction is startling. Put the gift down, right there, and walk away from the altar.

teach.b: Here are his words, in the King James Bible: “Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.”
Christians read this alongside another line, and the two pull in different directions.
View one leans on Matthew. Look who's upset: the brother has something against you. Jesus doesn't ask who's right.
He sends you first, and lets worship wait. Its best case: if everyone waits for the other to move, nobody ever does.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: NAME IT, THEN FORGIVE.
teach.b: View two leans on Luke, where Jesus says: “If thy brother trespass against thee, rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him.” Its best case: peace built on pretending isn't peace.
A real wrong gets named, and a real change matters, especially after serious harm.

teach.h: AS MUCH AS LIETH IN YOU.
teach.b: Both views live in the church, and Paul's letter to the Romans gives them common ground: “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.”
If it be possible: sometimes it isn't, or isn't safe, and nobody is asked to walk back into harm. As much as lieth in you: your part, not theirs.
Going first doesn't mean pretending. It means opening the door. That's the weekly check.

how: Some Christians review their relationships each week and try to make peace where they can; in some churches people share a sign of peace during the service, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians also have a sacrament of reconciliation, or confession.

o: making peace with someone, as far as it lies in you
a formal ruling on who was right in an argument
agreeing never to mention a past hurt again

games.q: two lines on making peace — tap the pairs.
p: rebuke, and if he repent, forgive
as much as lieth in you

s: in Matthew 5, Jesus says finish the offering first, then make peace
the order is the other way: leave there thy gift, first be reconciled, then come.
Jesus' example is about someone who has something against you
thy brother hath ought against thee. you go first anyway.
Paul says peace with everyone is always possible
he hedges it: if it be possible, as much as lieth in you.

games.q: your friend says: "go first, always, no matter what." she asks for the other view, from Luke 17, at its strongest. what do you say?
o: peace needs truth: name the wrong, and forgive when they turn.
never forgive anyone until they've paid back what they owe.
reconciling is optional; avoiding them is just as good.
games.why: Luke 17:3: rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him. its best case is that pretending isn't peace. Matthew's best case is that someone has to move first.

practice: Close your eyes and ask the question slowly: is there anyone I need to make peace with? Let a face come, without arguing the case.
Then choose one first step, an apology, a message, a returned call, or, where contact isn't safe, simply a prayer for them.

wordCard.voice: Reconciliation. Making peace, as far as it lies in you: going first, naming what's true, and letting the gift wait at the altar until you do.

orig.note: Greek for be reconciled, in Matthew 5:24.

carryVoice: Your line: first be reconciled. The gift can wait a little while; the door won't open by itself. Talk tomorrow.
